intro: Fourteen verses in three movements: what God has already done (2 to 4), what the community is asking for now (5 to 8), and an answer that is heard rather than requested (9 to 14). The root sh-v-b, turn or return, is the spine and appears in all three: You turned back the fortunes, You turned back from Your anger, turn us, will You not turn again, let them not turn back. Verse 11 is the line everyone knows, and it repays slow reading because both verbs are physical: two pairs of abstractions that meet in the street and kiss. In the cycle that reads the whole book across thirty days it falls on the seventeenth.

stichs.en: For the leader.
Of the sons of Korah, a psalm.

verses.summary: The heading assigns the psalm not to David but to the Korahite singers, the guild credited with a group of psalms that includes 42, 84 and 87.

stichs.en: You have shown favour to Your land, LORD,
You have brought back the fortunes of Jacob.

verses.summary: The psalm opens in the past tense, with what has already been done. Whether that past is a memory or a confidence about what is coming is the question the rest of it lives on.

stichs.en: You have carried away the guilt of Your people,
You have covered all their sin. Selah.

verses.summary: Two verbs for forgiveness, one of lifting and one of covering. Neither of them says the sin was small; both say it was moved out of sight.

stichs.en: You have gathered in all Your fury,
You have turned back from the heat of Your anger.

verses.summary: The anger is described as something collected up and put away, which is a physical image standing in for a change of mind.

stichs.en: Bring us back, God of our rescue,
and break off Your vexation with us.

verses.summary: The turn from report to request, and the first imperative in the psalm. The same root that said You turned back the fortunes now asks You to turn us.

stichs.en: Will You be angry with us for ever?
Will You drag Your anger out through every generation?

glosses: will it be for ever that
verses.summary: The politest possible complaint, put as two questions. Behind them sits the fear that the forgiveness reported in verse 3 was only temporary.

stichs.en: Will You not turn again and give us life,
so that Your people may rejoice in You?

verses.summary: The third question changes direction: not how long will this last, but will You not do the opposite. The reason offered is joy rather than merit.

stichs.en: Show us Your kindness, LORD,
and give us Your salvation.

verses.summary: The petition ends on two nouns, kindness and salvation, and both of them are picked up and reused by the answer that follows.

stichs.en: Let me hear what God the LORD will speak:
for He speaks peace to His people and to those faithful to Him,
and let them not go back to folly.

verses.summary: The speaker stops asking and listens. What comes next is quoted speech, and this verse announces its content before delivering it.

stichs.en: His rescue is close to those who fear Him,
so that glory may dwell in our land.

verses.summary: The answer opens with a condition attached to it: near to those who fear Him. The verb for dwelling is the one used of a presence settling in a sanctuary.

stichs.en: Kindness and truth have met,
righteousness and peace have kissed.

verses.summary: The famous line. Four abstract nouns behave like people running into each other in a street, and both verbs are about bodies rather than ideas.

stichs.en: Truth will spring up from the ground,
and righteousness will look down from the sky.

verses.summary: The meeting is given a geography. One quality grows up out of the soil like a crop, the other leans over an edge and looks down.

stichs.en: The LORD too will give what is good,
and our land will give its yield.

verses.summary: The abstractions come down to rain and harvest. The verb give is used twice in the same form, once of God and once of the ground.

stichs.en: Righteousness will walk ahead of Him,
and will make His footsteps into a road.

verses.summary: Righteousness goes in front as a herald and then turns into the road itself. The psalm closes on movement rather than on arrival.

pardes.body: Three movements and a change of posture. Verses 2 to 4 report five completed acts of favour: You favoured, You turned back, You lifted, You covered, You gathered in. Verses 5 to 8 then ask for what the first movement has just said already happened, which is the whole problem of the psalm in miniature. Verses 9 to 14 are an answer, introduced by a speaker who stops petitioning and listens. Whether the past tense of the opening is memory of a real return or the confident perfect of prophecy is the oldest question about this text, and the psalm does not resolve it. The verb at {{3.0}} is the ordinary word for picking up a load, so forgiveness here is weight carried off rather than weight cancelled.

The root sh-v-b, turn or return, is the spine, and each occurrence has a different subject: {{2.3}} in the report, {{5.0}} in the petition, {{7.2}} in the question, {{9.13}} in the warning. The sequence runs God, us, God, us. Verse 2 also carries a crux that translations show plainly. The two words at {{2.3}} and {{2.4}} are read either as returned the captivity, from the root for taking captive, or as restored the fortunes, from the root for turning, and the choice decides whether the psalm is remembering an exile or a change in the weather. It is disputed. The last three words of verse 9 are abrupt in Hebrew, and translators differ over whether {{9.14}} closes the divine speech or is the psalmist's own aside about his people.

The four nouns of verse 11 are the cast of a well known midrash. Bereshit Rabbah 8:5, commenting on the plural in let us make man at Genesis 1:26, has kindness, truth, righteousness and peace argue over whether the human being should be created at all; kindness and righteousness argue for it, truth and peace against, and truth is thrown to the ground. The very next verse here, {{12.2}}, truth will sprout from the earth, is read as what happens after the throwing. Taken that way the psalm is not describing four qualities that agree, it is describing four qualities reconciled after a quarrel, which is a harder and more interesting claim.

In the kabbalistic vocabulary the four terms of verse 11 are positions rather than qualities. Kindness and truth belong to the right side and the centre, righteousness names the receiving end of the structure and peace the channel that reaches it, so {{11.2}} and {{11.5}}, met and kissed, describe a joining rather than an agreement reached in an argument. The two directions of verse 12 hold the same picture from another angle: something rising from below and something inclining from above. In this reading the human contribution is the sprouting one, and nothing arrives from above that was not first grown from underneath.
